title: Personal narrative: telling a true story in order

vocabulary.definition: a story that tells what happened, in order
the order in which events happen
a small piece of information that helps the reader picture the story
the exact words people say in a story, shown inside quotation marks
a word that tells the reader when something happened, such as first, next or finally
a person or animal in a story; in a true story, the writer is a character too
an emotion, such as nervous, proud or excited
quickly and without warning

L3-4: One day, I ___ with my ___.
When ___, I felt ___ because ___.
Suddenly, ___.
At the end, ___, and I felt ___.
L5-6: My heart ___ when ___, and I thought, "___."
The ___ smelled like ___, which reminded me of ___.
"___," ___ said, and that is when I realized ___.
Looking back, I learned that ___.

activity.title: Story Hand: Plan, Say, Write
steps: Model with a short true story of your own, for example: 'First, my aunt handed me a bowl of dough. Then I tried to roll it flat, but it kept sticking. Suddenly, she laughed and sprinkled flour on my nose. Finally, I made my first round, warm bread, and I felt proud.' Students listen for and count the transition words on their fingers.
Trace a hand on paper. Label the fingers: who and where, first, then, suddenly (the big moment), finally. Write the feeling word in the palm.

Students choose one small true moment: cooking with a family member, a first day somewhere new, a game, a celebration, a pet, a trip, learning to do something. They sketch or write two or three words on each finger.
Partners take turns telling their story aloud, touching each finger as they go. The listener asks one question: 'What did you see?' or 'How did you feel?' The teller adds that detail.
Students write their story, one or two sentences per finger, using the frames for their band. Challenge writers add one line of dialogue with quotation marks.
Partners reread each other's stories and underline every transition word and circle the feeling word. Two volunteers share aloud.

title: Argument writing: claims, evidence and counterclaims

vocabulary.definition: the main position a writer argues for and tries to prove
facts, data, examples or expert statements that support a reason
a position that disagrees with the writer's claim
the part of an argument that answers a counterclaim and shows why the claim is still stronger
closely connected to the point being made
able to be trusted or believed
to admit that something is true or deserves attention
to convince someone to believe or do something

L1-2: I think school should start ___. (later / at the same time)
L3-4: Middle school should ___ because ___.
According to ___, ___. This shows that ___.
Although some people think ___, ___.
Therefore, ___.
L5-6: The strongest reason to ___ is ___, as shown by ___.
This evidence matters because it demonstrates that ___, which means ___.
Opponents may argue that ___; however, this concern overlooks ___.
While ___ is a fair point, a better solution would be ___ because ___.

activity.title: Evidence Sort and Build
steps: Pose the question: 'Should our middle school start one hour later?' Students take a 30-second stand by writing yes or no on a sticky note.

Give each pair four evidence cards (sample information written for this lesson): A) In a survey of 200 students at one school, 140 said they feel sleepy in first period. B) Doctors recommend that people ages 13 to 18 get 8 to 10 hours of sleep. C) The school's soccer team won four games this fall. D) A later start could push after-school practices and jobs later into the evening.

Partners sort the cards into relevant to yes, relevant to no and not relevant, and explain each choice aloud with 'This card is relevant because ___.' (Card C is not relevant; card D is a counterclaim.)
Partners solve the problem below so they can state the survey result as a percent in their writing.
Each student writes a paragraph: claim, one reason, evidence introduced with According to or shows that, one or two sentences of commentary, then a concession sentence (Although ___) and a rebuttal.
Pairs swap paragraphs and highlight the reporting verb in one color and the concession word in another. If either is missing, the writer revises one sentence before sharing.

problems.prompt: On card A, 140 of 200 surveyed students said they feel sleepy in first period. What percent of the students is that?

vocabulary.definition: the number of square units that cover a flat shape
a side of a shape chosen to measure from; the height is measured perpendicular to it
the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite side or vertex
meeting at a right angle
a four-sided shape with two pairs of parallel sides
a four-sided shape with at least one pair of parallel sides
to break a shape into smaller shapes
to move pieces into a new position without changing their size

L1-2: I cut the shape into a ___ and a ___.
The height is perpendicular / not perpendicular. (Word bank: base, height, triangle, rectangle, cut, move)
L3-4: I decomposed the ___ into ___ and ___, so the area is ___ + ___.
The area of the triangle is half of the ___ because ___.
I agree / disagree with ___ because the height should be ___.
L5-6: Moving this triangle does not change the area, because ___; it only changes ___.
I see why you used ___, but ___, so the area would actually be ___.
Both decompositions give ___ square units because ___, even though one uses ___ and the other uses ___.

activity.title: Cut, Slide, Defend
steps: Give each group of three paper copies of a parallelogram (base 9 m, height 4 m, slanted side 5 m), a trapezoid and an L-shaped garden, plus scissors.
Each student takes one shape, cuts it into pieces and rearranges or splits it so the area can be found from rectangles and triangles. They write the area with square units.
In turn, each student presents with I decomposed ___ into ___ and if/so reasoning. The other two must each ask one question or raise one disagreement using a critique frame.
Show a sample error: someone found the parallelogram's area as 9 × 5. Groups agree or disagree in writing and fix it.
Groups solve the problems below, then share one case where two members decomposed the same shape differently and still got the same area.

problems.prompt: A right triangle has legs of 8 cm and 5 cm. What is its area?
A parallelogram has a base of 9 m, a height of 4 m and a slanted side of 5 m. What is its area?
A trapezoid has parallel sides of 6 ft and 10 ft and a height of 4 ft. Decompose it to find its area.
An L-shaped garden is a 10 m by 6 m rectangle with a 4 m by 3 m corner removed. What is its area?

vocabulary.definition: the quantity that changes on its own or is chosen first; it goes on the horizontal axis
the quantity whose value depends on the independent variable; it goes on the vertical axis
to change because of something else; to rely on
the way two quantities are connected
to become greater
to get money for work
a picture that shows how two quantities are related, using points on axes

L1-2: e = ___ × d. (Word bank: dogs, dollars, depends on, increase)
L3-4: The dependent variable is ___ because it changes when ___ changes.
As ___ increases by 1, ___ increases by ___.
In the equation e = 6d, the 6 means ___.
L5-6: It would not make sense to say ___ depends on ___, because ___.
The table, the graph and the equation all show ___: in the table ___, on the graph ___, and in the equation ___.
Using the equation, I predict ___ when ___ is ___, which I can check on the graph by ___.

activity.title: Dog-Walking Business
steps: Read the story: Mia earns $6 for each dog she walks. Partners decide which quantity depends on which and say it with a frame before writing anything.
Partner A builds a table for 0 to 5 dogs; Partner B plots the points on a grid with dogs on the horizontal axis and dollars on the vertical axis.
Partners trade papers and each describes the pattern in the other's representation with As ___ increases by 1, ___ increases by ___.
Together they write the equation e = 6d and explain what the 6 means in all three representations. Then they solve the problems below.
Repeat the dependence talk quickly for the road-trip problem, then share: Why can't we say the number of dogs depends on her earnings?

problems.prompt: Mia earns $6 for each dog she walks. Write an equation for her earnings e in terms of the number of dogs d. How much does she earn for 7 dogs?
How many dogs must Mia walk to earn $54?
A car travels at a constant 55 miles per hour. How far does it travel in 3.5 hours?
In the car problem, which quantity is the independent variable?
problems.answer: Time in hours; the distance depends on how long the car travels.

title: Dividing fractions: how many groups, how much in one group

vocabulary.definition: the answer to a division problem
the amount being divided; the first number in a ÷ b
the number you divide by; the size of one group or the number of groups
the number that multiplies with a given number to make 1; the reciprocal of 3/4 is 4/3
a set of things counted together as one
the amount for one person or one use, such as one serving
to go into a space exactly; how many times one amount goes into another

L1-2: It is ___ groups. (Word bank: groups, fit, cup, three-fourths, one-eighth)
L3-4: This story asks how many ___ are in ___, so I divide ___ by ___.
My tape diagram shows that ___ fits into ___ ___ times.
Since each ___ is ___, ___ makes ___.
L5-6: The quotient is greater than the dividend because the divisor is less than 1, which means ___.
This story asks how much is in one whole group, so ___ ÷ ___ tells ___.
Multiplying by the reciprocal works here because ___, and my model confirms it by ___.

activity.title: Kitchen Division Stories
steps: Groups of three get the three story cards below and a strip of paper for tape diagrams. Roles: Reader, Modeler, Explainer; rotate for each card.
The Reader reads the card aloud. Everyone sorts it on the mat: How many groups? or How much in one group? The Explainer names the words in the story that decided it.
The Modeler folds or marks the paper strip to show the story, saying the division as a question (How many one-eighths are in three-fourths?).
The Explainer states the answer with a since/so sentence. Only then does the group check with the reciprocal and compare the two methods.
Exit talk: each group answers why 3 ÷ 3/4 is bigger than 3, using one frame from the L5-6 band if possible.

problems.prompt: You have 3 cups of yogurt. Each smoothie uses 3/4 cup. How many smoothies can you make?
How many 1/8-cup scoops of cocoa are in 3/4 cup?
Four-fifths of a bag of flour weighs 2 pounds. How much does a full bag weigh?
problems.answer: 2.5 pounds, or two and a half pounds

vocabulary.definition: a rate per 100; 30% means 30 out of every 100
a piece of the whole; in a percent problem, the amount that matches the percent
the full amount that stands for 100%
an amount taken off the original price
a familiar value used to estimate or check, such as 50% for half
a rectangle split into equal sections to show parts of a whole
two number lines that line up equivalent amounts, such as percents above and quantities below
one of 100 equal parts of a whole

L1-2: ___ out of 100 squares are shaded. That is ___%.
The whole is ___. The part is ___. (Word bank: whole, part, percent, of, off)
L3-4: First, I found 10% of ___, which is ___. Then I ___.
___ is ___% of ___, because each 10% of the tape stands for ___.
The jacket is ___% off, so I subtract ___ from the original price.
L5-6: Since ___% means ___ per 100, I can scale the ratio ___ : 100 to ___ : ___.
The question asks for the ___, not the ___, so after finding ___ I still need to ___.
Another way to check is to use the benchmark ___%, which tells me ___.

activity.title: Hundred-Grid Sale Talk
steps: Give each pair a 10-by-10 grid and a blank tape divided into 10 equal sections. Write 100% under the end of the tape and $40 above it.
Partner A shades 25 squares and says, 25 out of 100, so 25%. Partner B labels the tape: each section is 10% and stands for $4.
Together, partners solve the jacket problems below. One partner explains each step aloud with First / Then / So; the other writes only after hearing the explanation.
Swap roles for the class survey problem and the find-the-whole problem. The writer must name the whole, the part and the percent in the margin before writing an answer.
Quick check: hold up of or off cards while you read three short sale phrases; partners explain one choice to the class.

problems.prompt: A jacket costs $40 and is 25% off. How many dollars do you save?
What is the sale price of the jacket?
In a class of 30 students, 60% walk to school. How many students walk?
Twelve students chose soccer. That is 20% of the grade. How many students are in the grade?

vocabulary.definition: a flat surface made by a horizontal number line and a vertical number line crossing at 0
one of the two number lines on the coordinate plane; the plural is axes
the point (0, 0) where the axes cross
one of the four regions the axes divide the plane into
two numbers (x, y) that give the location of a point; the order matters
going straight left and right, like the horizon
going straight up and down
to flip a point across a line so it lands the same distance away on the other side

L1-2: Start at the origin. Move ___ units left / right.
The point is in Quadrant ___. (Word bank: left, right, up, down, origin, axis)
L3-4: The point (___, ___) is in Quadrant ___ because x is ___ and y is ___.
Start at the origin, move ___ units ___, then ___ units ___.
Point ___ is a reflection of point ___ across the ___-axis.
L5-6: Since only the sign of the ___-coordinate changed, the point reflected across the ___-axis and stayed ___ units from it.
Your point is off because you moved along the ___ first; the x-coordinate always tells ___.
Both points are ___ units from the origin horizontally, but they lie in different quadrants because ___.

activity.title: Hidden Point Directions
steps: Partners sit with a folder standing between them. Each has a blank coordinate plane from −6 to 6 on both axes.
Partner A secretly plots a point in Quadrant II, III or IV and gives directions using the frames. Partner B plots it without looking and reads back the ordered pair.
Lower the folder and compare. If the plots differ, Partner A names the step that went wrong (You moved up before you moved left). Switch roles; play four rounds.
Round 5: Partner A gives a point, Partner B plots its reflection across the y-axis, then across the x-axis, and describes what changed and what stayed the same.
Partners solve the problems below and share one description of a reflection with the class.

problems.prompt: Plot the point (−3, 4). Which quadrant is it in?
problems.answer: Quadrant II: left of the y-axis and above the x-axis.

problems.prompt: Point A is at (−5, 2). Point B is its reflection across the y-axis. What is the x-coordinate of point B?
problems.answer: 5, the same distance from the y-axis on the right side

problems.prompt: On a town map with the school at the origin, the library is at (−4, 3) and the park is at (6, 3). How many blocks apart are they along the street?

title: Positive and negative numbers in context

vocabulary.definition: a number greater than 0
a number less than 0, written with a − sign
a number the same distance from 0 on the other side, such as 7 and −7
the average height of the ocean's surface, used as 0 for elevation
how high or low a place is compared with sea level
money put into an account; shown with a positive number
money taken out of an account; shown with a negative number
to stand for or show something

L1-2: Zero means ___. (Word bank: sea level, freezing, no money, start)
L3-4: In this situation, positive means ___ and negative means ___.
___ represents ___ because ___.
Here, 0 stands for ___, so a number below 0 shows ___.
L5-6: I chose ___ as the positive direction because ___; the opposite, ___, is negative.
Although both numbers have the same distance from 0, ___ and ___ describe opposite ___.
Zero is not the absence of a quantity here; it is the reference point where ___.

activity.title: Opposites Gallery
steps: Post four context cards around the room: a diver and a bird over the ocean, a thermometer, a bank app, a football field. Each card has a vertical number line.
At each card, Partner A chooses the positive direction and says it with a frame; Partner B says what 0 means for that card. They write both on a sticky note.
Partners write one signed number for the card's situation and the full description (−18 represents 18 feet below sea level). Rotate after about 2 minutes.
Back at seats, partners solve the problems below, reading every signed number aloud as negative or positive, not minus.
Share: read sticky notes from one card aloud and compare how different pairs defined 0.

problems.prompt: A diver is at −18 feet. A bird is flying 25 feet above sea level. How many feet apart are they vertically?
At noon the temperature was 5°C. At midnight it was −3°C. How many degrees did the temperature fall?
A football team loses seven yards on a play. Write the signed number in words and explain what 0 means.
problems.answer: Negative seven yards; zero means the ball stayed at the line where the play started, with no gain and no loss.

vocabulary.definition: a comparison of two quantities, such as 4 scoops of peanuts to 6 scoops of raisins
an amount that can be counted or measured
for each group of; used to link the two amounts in a ratio
a ratio that compares one part of a group to another part of the same group
a ratio that compares one part of a group to the whole group
ratios that describe the same relationship, such as 4 to 6 and 2 to 3
to look at two things to see how they are alike or different

L1-2: For every ___ peanuts, there are ___ raisins.
Part-to-part or part-to-whole? It is ___. (Word bank: part, whole, total, to)
L3-4: The ratio of ___ to ___ is ___ to ___ because ___.
For every ___, there are ___, so for ___, there would be ___.
This is a part-to-whole ratio because ___ is the total number of ___.
L5-6: The ratio ___:___ stays the same in every row because both quantities are multiplied by ___.
If we reversed the order to ___ to ___, the statement would mean ___ instead.
Both ratios use the numbers ___ and ___, but one compares ___ and the other compares ___.

activity.title: Trail Mix Ratio Talk
steps: Show the recipe card: one batch of trail mix is 4 scoops of peanuts and 6 scoops of raisins. Draw it as 4 brown circles and 6 purple circles.

Partner A says one ratio with a frame (For every 4 peanuts, there are 6 raisins). Partner B names it part-to-part or part-to-whole, then says it in reverse order and tells what the new order means. Switch roles twice.
Partners build a table with columns Peanuts and Raisins: 2 and 3, 4 and 6, then fill in 6, 8 and 10 scoops of peanuts. Each partner explains one row aloud using times as many or for every.
Partners solve the problems below. Before writing an answer, each partner says the ratio statement the answer comes from.
Share out: two pairs read one sentence each; the class checks that the quantities are in the stated order and that each number has a unit.

problems.prompt: The recipe uses 4 scoops of peanuts for every 6 scoops of raisins. How many scoops of raisins go with 10 scoops of peanuts?
How many scoops are in one batch in all? Use that total to say the part-to-whole ratio of peanuts to all scoops.
problems.answer: 10 scoops in all, so peanuts to the whole batch is four to ten (or two to five)

problems.prompt: A class has 12 girls and 18 boys. Complete the statement: for every 2 girls, there are ___ boys.

vocabulary.definition: about collecting and studying data that varies
how much the answers in a data set differ from each other
facts or numbers collected to answer a question
one answer or measurement in a data set
a set of questions asked to a group to collect data
to be different from one to another
to say what you think will happen before it happens

L1-2: The answers will be the same / different.
It is / is not a statistical question. (Word bank: vary, same, different, survey, data)
L3-4: This question is / is not statistical because the answers would / would not vary.
I would ask ___, and the answers might range from ___ to ___.
To make it statistical, I changed ___ to ___.
L5-6: Although this question has a number for an answer, it is not statistical, because ___.
The revised question anticipates variability, since ___; I would expect answers such as ___ and ___.
My data set would have about ___ observations of ___, measured in ___.

activity.title: Statistical or Not? Card Sort
steps: Each pair gets eight question cards, such as How tall is the classroom door? and How many minutes did students in our class read last night?
Partners take turns drawing a card, predicting two possible answers aloud, and placing it on the Statistical or Not Statistical side with a because sentence.
For every Not Statistical card, partners rewrite it as a statistical question and tell who they would ask and what would vary.
Partners choose one revised question and describe the data set: attribute, unit and number of observations if they asked the whole class.
Partners solve the problems below; two pairs share a revision and the class predicts the range of answers.

problems.prompt: Statistical or not: How tall is the classroom door?
problems.answer: Not statistical; there is one correct measurement, so no variability is expected.

problems.prompt: Revise this question so it is statistical: How old is Ms. Rivera?
problems.answer: Possible answer: How old are the teachers at our school? The answers will vary from teacher to teacher.

problems.prompt: A class asked, How many minutes did you read last night? The answers were 0, 15, 20, 20, 30, 45 and 60. How many observations were collected?
For the same data, what is the difference between the greatest and least answers?

title: Unit rates and the better buy

vocabulary.definition: a ratio that compares two quantities with different units, such as miles and hours
a rate that tells the amount for 1 of the second quantity, such as $0.25 per ounce
the price for one unit of measure, such as one ounce or one pound
how far something travels in a unit of time
staying the same; not changing
to split a quantity into equal groups or find how many groups fit
an offer to buy something; a better deal gives more for the same money
every one, taken one at a time

L1-2: The ___ box is the better buy. (big / small)
One ounce costs ___. (Word bank: per, each, ounce, costs less)
L3-4: I divided ___ by ___ to find the cost of one ___.
The ___ box costs $___ per ounce, but the ___ box costs $___ per ounce.
The ___ box is the better buy because it costs less for each ___.
L5-6: Even though the ___ box has a higher total price, its unit price is lower, because ___.
To compare fairly, both rates have to be in ___ per ___, so I ___.
At a constant rate of ___ per ___, in ___ we would expect ___, since ___.

activity.title: Best Buy Showdown
steps: Show two cereal boxes: Box A is 12 ounces for $3.00; Box B is 18 ounces for $3.96. Ask each pair for a quick gut claim: which is the better buy?
Partner A finds the unit price of Box A and Partner B finds Box B. Each says the division aloud with a frame (I divided ___ by ___ to find the cost of one ___).
Partners write a claim and two pieces of evidence on a sticky note. One partner argues for the other box on purpose; the other answers the counterclaim using unit price, not total price.
Switch contexts: a student walks 6 miles in 2 hours at a constant speed. Partners find the unit rate and use it to predict the distance in 5 hours (6.RP.A.3b).
Two pairs read their claim aloud; the class listens for per plus a singular unit and for both rates being in the same unit.

problems.prompt: Box A holds 12 ounces of cereal and costs $3.00. What is its unit price?
Box B holds 18 ounces of cereal and costs $3.96. What is its unit price?
Which box is the better buy? Support your claim with the unit prices.
problems.answer: Box B, the larger box, because it costs less per ounce than Box A.

problems.prompt: A student walks 6 miles in 2 hours at a constant speed. At that rate, how far will the student walk in 5 hours?

vocabulary.definition: a math sentence with an equal sign showing that two amounts are the same
the value of the variable that makes the equation true
to put a number in place of a variable
an operation that undoes another, such as subtraction undoing addition
the amount you do not know yet; the variable stands for it
the left and right parts of an equation, on either side of the equal sign
a state where two sides are equal; an equation is like a balanced scale

L1-2: Let x be the number of ___.
x = ___. (Word bank: add, subtract, multiply, divide, both sides)
L3-4: Let ___ be ___. The equation is ___ because ___.
I ___ both sides by ___ to get ___ by itself.
To check, I put ___ back in: ___, so my solution is correct.
L5-6: This story is an addition equation, not a multiplication equation, because ___.
Using the inverse operation keeps the equation balanced, since whatever I do to one side ___.
My solution makes sense in the story because ___; a value like ___ would not, since ___.

activity.title: Story to Equation Relay
steps: Each pair gets the four story cards below and a balance-scale mat. Partner A is the Writer and Partner B is the Checker; switch after each card.
The Writer reads the story aloud and says Let ___ be ___ before writing anything. The Checker confirms the unit is included.

The Writer writes the equation and solves it, saying the inverse operation aloud. The Checker substitutes the answer into the equation and into the story and says Correct because ___ or Not yet because ___.
After all four cards, partners sort them into addition equations and multiplication equations and explain one card in each group.
Share: one pair explains the flour card, where the numbers are fractions but the steps are the same.

problems.prompt: Jamal had some stickers. His friend gave him 12 more, and now he has 41. How many stickers did he have at first?
Five notebooks cost $8.75 in all, and each costs the same. What is the price of one notebook?
A recipe needs 2 1/4 cups of flour. Rosa has 3/4 cup. How much more flour does she need?
problems.answer: 1.5 cups, or one and a half cups

problems.prompt: Each lap around the track is 3/4 mile. Lena ran 6 miles. How many laps did she run?

vocabulary.definition: a letter that stands for a number
numbers, letters and operation signs with no equal sign, such as 3x + 4
a part of an expression separated by + or −, such as 3x or 4 in 3x + 4
the number multiplied by a variable; in 14t it is 14
the result of multiplying
to find the value of an expression by replacing each letter with a number
subtracted from; 7 less than n means n − 7
two times

L1-2: When n is ___, the answer is ___.
The variable is ___. (Word bank: plus, minus, times, less than, more than)
L3-4: The phrase ___ means ___ because the word ___ tells me to ___.
When ___ is ___, the expression ___ equals ___.
In this expression, ___ is the coefficient and it means ___.
L5-6: The order is reversed in ___ because than / from signals that ___ comes first.
Without parentheses, ___ would mean ___, so the grouping changes the value from ___ to ___.
The term ___ represents ___ in the story, while the constant ___ represents ___.

activity.title: Say It, Write It, Check It
steps: Each pair gets eight cards: four word phrases (7 less than n, the product of 5 and m, subtract y from 20, three times the sum of x and 4) and four expressions to match.
Partner A reads a phrase aloud; Partner B writes the expression without seeing the card, then explains which word told them the operation and the order. Switch after each card.
Partners flip to the expression side, and Partner B reads one aloud for Partner A to write. Compare with the card; fix any grouping error by saying where the pause belongs.
Partners solve the problems below. For each evaluation, say the full sentence (When t is 4, ...) before writing the value.
Close by having one pair explain why 7 less than n is not 7 − n.

problems.prompt: Write an expression for 7 less than n. Then evaluate it when n = 20.
Evaluate 3(x + 4) when x = 6.
A movie ticket costs $9 and popcorn costs $5. Write an expression for the total cost when t friends each buy a ticket and popcorn, and evaluate it for t = 4.

vocabulary.definition: the breaking down of rock into smaller pieces by water, ice, wind, plants or chemicals
the moving of rock pieces and soil from one place to another by water, ice, wind or gravity
small bits of rock, sand and soil that are carried and then dropped
a huge, slow-moving body of ice that scrapes and carries rock
ground that goes up or down at an angle, like the side of a hill
how fast something happens over a period of time
facts or measurements that show an idea is true

L3-4: The sand moved because ___.
After ___ pours, the sand moved ___ centimeters, so ___.
___ is weathering, but ___ is erosion because ___.
On the steep slope, the sand moved ___ than on the gentle slope.
L5-6: Our measurements show that ___, which is evidence that ___.
Although water touched both slopes, the steep slope lost more sand because ___.
First the water ___; as a result, ___; finally, the sediment ___.
If we poured the water faster, I predict ___, because ___.

activity.title: Sand Slope Race
steps: Before class, pack damp sand at one end of two trays. Prop one tray on a book (gentle slope) and one on three books (steep slope). Tape a paper ruler along each tray.
Hold up a cracked rock and a cup of sand. Ask: 'Which shows breaking? Which shows moving?' Post the anchor: weathering = break; erosion = move.
A volunteer slowly pours the same cup of water at the top of each tray three times. Groups record, in centimeters, how far the front edge of the sand traveled after each pour.
Groups compare their two numbers and complete one L1-2, L3-4 or L5-6 frame aloud with a partner before anyone writes.
Each student writes two sentences: one cause-and-effect sentence (because / so / as a result) and one comparative sentence that includes a measurement.
Close by asking one group to explain how this tray models a real river or a hillside after a storm, and add one new word to the class word wall.

problems.prompt: The sand pile was 12 centimeters tall before pouring and 7 centimeters tall after. How many centimeters of height did the pile lose?
On the steep slope the sand moved 18 centimeters in 3 pours. On average, how many centimeters did it move per pour?
The sand moved 18 centimeters on the steep slope and 11 centimeters on the gentle slope. How much farther did it move on the steep slope?

vocabulary.definition: all the living things in an area and the nonliving things they depend on, working together
all the members of one species living in the same area at the same time
something living things need and use, such as food, water or shelter
a resource or condition that keeps a population from growing larger
when organisms try to get the same limited resource
present in large amounts; more than enough
to become smaller in number or amount; a decrease
the general direction in which data change over time

L1-2: My claim: Squirrels need ___ to survive.
L3-4: As the acorn crop ___, the squirrel population ___ the next spring.
My evidence is that in Year ___, ___, but in Year ___, ___.
This happens because acorns are a limiting factor, so when they are scarce, ___.
Someone might say ___, but the table shows ___.
L5-6: The data suggest that ___; for example, between Year ___ and Year ___, the population showed a ___ percent change.
Because the population responds one season after the crop, ___.
One might argue that ___; however, the pattern across all four years indicates ___.
To make this claim stronger, scientists could also measure ___, because ___.

activity.title: Data Detectives: Acorns and Squirrels
steps: Project this table (sample data from an imaginary oak forest): Fall acorn crop in kg per hectare / squirrels counted the next spring. Year 1: 200 / 80. Year 2: 50 / 48. Year 3: 220 / 88. Year 4: 120 / 64.
Partners spend two minutes noticing: draw an up or down arrow beside each number that changed from the year before, then say one sentence using a trend verb (rose, dropped, peaked, recovered).
Partners solve the three problems below, then circle the two rows that give the strongest evidence.
Each partner writes a claim, two pieces of numerical evidence and one sentence of reasoning that uses the term limiting factor. Point students to the frame that matches their band.

Hand each pair a challenge card: 'A hawk family moved into the forest in Year 2. Maybe the hawks caused the drop.' Partners add one sentence that acknowledges this idea and one that uses Year 3 or Year 4 to respond.
Two pairs read their arguments aloud; the class names which hedge word (suggest, likely, possible) each pair used and whether it matched the strength of the evidence.

problems.prompt: The squirrel population went from 80 in Year 1 to 48 in Year 2. What was the percent decrease?
The acorn crop went from 200 kg per hectare in Year 1 to 50 kg per hectare in Year 2. What was the percent decrease?
How many fewer squirrels were counted in Year 4 than in Year 3?

title: Maps, regions and the language of comparison

vocabulary.definition: an area whose places share features such as landforms, climate or culture
the box on a map that explains what each symbol and color means; also called a map key
the usual weather of a place over many years
a natural shape of the land, such as a mountain, valley, plain or plateau
how high a place is above sea level
a line that shows where one place ends and another begins
a feature that helps describe or identify something
to look at how two or more things are alike and different

L1-2: Region A has ___. (mountains / a coast / rivers)
Region B is ___. (dry / wet / high / low)
Region A is ___ of Region B. (north / south / east / west)
L3-4: Region A is ___ than Region B.
Both regions ___, but Region A ___.
The legend shows that ___ means ___.
Region B is located ___, so ___.
L5-6: While Region A ___, Region B ___, which affects how people ___.
According to the map and the table, the greatest difference between the regions is ___.
Region A gets ___ centimeters more rain each year than Region B, so ___.
Although both regions ___, they differ in ___ because ___.

activity.title: Region Detectives
steps: Display a practice map of an imaginary country with a legend. Region A, in the east, is a low coastal plain with rivers and farms. Region B, in the west, is a dry, mountainous plateau. Show this table beside it: Average yearly rainfall: Region A 120 cm, Region B 25 cm. Highest elevation: Region A 50 m, Region B 1,500 m.
Point to three legend symbols and have students tell a partner what each one means: 'This symbol means ___.'
Partners fold a paper into a T-chart labeled Region A and Region B, with rows for location, landforms, climate and how people might live. They fill in each row using words or quick sketches.
Partners solve the two problems below and add the answers to the climate and landforms rows.
Partners circle one similarity (for example, both have a border with the same neighbor country, or both have rivers) and say it aloud with 'Both regions ___.'

Each student writes three sentences: one similarity, one difference with a comparative and one sentence that uses while or but. Students who have lived in or visited another region or country may add a sentence comparing it to where they live now.

problems.prompt: Region A gets 120 centimeters of rain each year. Region B gets 25 centimeters. How many more centimeters of rain does Region A get?
The highest point in Region B is 1500 meters above sea level. The highest point in Region A is 50 meters. How much higher is Region B's highest point?

title: Civic participation and arguing a local issue

vocabulary.definition: related to the duties and activities of people in a community or country
a person or group affected by a decision who has an interest in how it turns out
a written request signed by many people and sent to leaders, asking for a change
the group of elected officials who make laws and decisions for a city
the way a person sees an issue, shaped by their experiences and interests
to speak or act in support of an idea or a group
an agreement in which each side gives up part of what it wants
to judge how good, strong or useful something is

L1-2: It helps ___. (families / shops / students / older neighbors)
L3-4: The city council should ___ because ___.
If the lot becomes a ___, then ___.
From the perspective of ___, ___.
___'s argument was convincing because ___.
L5-6: Although ___ have a valid concern about ___, the council should ___ because ___.
A fair compromise might be ___, which would address both ___ and ___.
___'s argument was one-sided because it did not consider ___.
Community members who want this outcome could ___, since that would let officials hear ___.

activity.title: Community Lot Hearing
steps: Set the scene: 'An empty lot sits next to the bus stop on Maple Street. The city council will decide whether it becomes a community garden or a parking lot, and tonight it is holding a public hearing.' Explain that many ways to take part, such as speaking during public comment, writing to council members or volunteering, are often open to community members whether or not they can vote.

Give each group four role cards: a grandmother who walks to the bus stop and wants space to grow vegetables with her grandchildren; a bakery owner whose customers cannot find parking; a student who wants a safe place to volunteer after school; a city planner who reports that parking spaces would bring in money for street repairs.

Each student reads one role card and has three minutes to prepare a 30-second public comment using the frames for their band. Each comment must include a should sentence and an If ___, then ___ sentence.

Run the hearing: one student acts as council chair and calls each speaker. Listeners score each comment on a quick checklist: relevant reason, specific detail, considers another group (one check each).

Groups deliberate for three minutes and agree on a recommendation, which may be a compromise (for example, a garden with a few short-term parking spaces). One member reports the decision and the most convincing argument they heard.

Each student writes a four-sentence recommendation to the council that names one way a community member could share it (letter, public comment or petition) and attributes at least one other stakeholder's perspective.
